To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) neutral stability in deterministic Lotka-Volterra models leads to extinction of species in stochastic models on a time scale that is proportional to the population sizes, and that (ii) the extinction probability can be computed by reduction of the stochastic model to a lower-dimensional deterministic effective model, which can be solved analytically in the case of two species.

(i) the survival of interacting populations is governed by the interplay of nonlinear deterministic dynamics and random fluctuations, (ii) in the neutral stability case, the latter dominate, leading to extinction of interacting populations, (iii) the dynamics of the population size is governed by an effective stochastic differential equation that is analytically tractable in the case of two interacting species, and (iv) this effective dynamics allows for a detailed understanding of the process of extinction of interacting species.

1) the survival of species in neutral Lotka-Volterra systems is governed by a stochastic process that is a diffusion process with drift; 2) the extinction time of the system is exponentially distributed; 3) the extinction rate is proportional to the total population size; 4) the effective dynamics is a diffusion process that can be solved analytically for highly symmetrical systems and can be solved numerically for systems that are not highly symmetrical.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the extinction of species in a stochastic environment.
the interplay of deterministic selection and stochastic fluctuations and provides a new approach to extinction phenomena in stochastic Lotka-Voltterra models.
the study of stochastic population dynamics in the context of competing biological species.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
stochasticity is the dominant factor in the extinction process in neutral systems, whereas in the case of instability, the deterministic part of the dynamics plays the dominant role.
the extinction of interacting populations is governed by a stochastic averaging process.
, if the deterministic dynamics of a population is neutral, then the stochastic dynamics is always unstable and leads to extinction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the stochastic dynamics of a population of interacting species can be reduced to the effective dynamics of an interacting pair of species.
the stochastic Lotka-Voltterra models with neutral stability are not robust to noise.
the stochastic dynamics of a system can be very different from its deterministic counterpart, even if the latter is neutral stable.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the stochasticity of biological interactions can have a profound impact on the survival of a species.
, in contrast to the deterministic dynamics, the extinction of a population in stochastic systems is a non-equilibrium process.
, in contrast to the case of positive stability, neutral stability is a very delicate property of a population dynamics model that can be easily disrupted by noise.
